title: 22. Interview: Vector Clocks
summary: Interview Q&A for Vector Clocks — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Vector Clocks interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Define the happens-before relation in terms of vector clocks and explain why it cannot be captured by wall-clock timestamps.
**Answer:** Event A happens-before event B (A `→` B) iff for every component `i`, `V_A[i] <= V_B[i]`, and `V_A != V_B` (at least one strictly less). This captures causal ordering: A could have influenced B through a chain of messages and local events. Wall-clock timestamps cannot capture this because (1) clock drift makes two events on different nodes have arbitrary relative order — A could send a message at physical time T1, B receives it at T0 < T1 due to B's clock being behind, falsely suggesting B happened first; (2) leap seconds and NTP corrections can jump clocks backwards, breaking monotonicity; (3) even with perfectly synchronized clocks, two events that are microseconds apart may be truly concurrent (no causal chain) but appear ordered by timestamp. The vector clock encodes causality directly through the message-passing structure: each event's vector is the join (per-component max) of all vectors that flowed into it, so two events are causally ordered iff one's information reached the other. The trade-off is that vector clocks are O(N) in size and require each node to know the full membership, whereas a wall-clock timestamp is O(1) but unreliable.
**Visual:**
```
A -> B iff V_A[i] <= V_B[i] for all i, AND V_A != V_B
A || B iff neither A->B nor B->A (concurrent)

Wall-clock fails:
  A sends at T=100 (A's clock)
  B receives at T=99 (B's clock slow)
  -> timestamps suggest B before A, but A caused B (causally A->B)
Vector clocks: B's vector dominates A's -> correctly A->B
```

### Q2. Contrast vector clocks with Lamport clocks. What can vector clocks do that Lamport clocks cannot?
**Answer:** A Lamport clock assigns each event a single integer `L = max(local, received) + 1`. It preserves causality in one direction: if A `→` B then `L(A) < L(B)`. The converse is **not** true: `L(A) < L(B)` does not imply A `→` B — A and B could be concurrent with B simply having a higher counter. Lamport clocks therefore impose a total order that loses concurrency information; you cannot look at two Lamport timestamps and tell whether the events were causally ordered or concurrent. Vector clocks, by contrast, encode the full causality structure: A `→` B iff V_A is component-wise ≤ V_B (and unequal), and concurrent events have incomparable vectors. The trade-off is cost: a Lamport clock is O(1) per event (one integer), while a vector clock is O(N) per event (one entry per node). For systems that need to detect conflicts (Dynamo, Riak, collaborative editors), Lamport clocks are insufficient and vector clocks are mandatory. For systems that only need a consistent ordering of events (mutual exclusion, snapshot coordination), Lamport clocks suffice and are far cheaper. The architect's choice: vector clocks when you must distinguish causal from concurrent; Lamport when you only need an order.
**Visual:**
```
Lamport: L = max(L_local, L_msg) + 1   (single int)
  A -> B  implies  L(A) < L(B)
  L(A) < L(B)  does NOT imply A->B  (could be concurrent)
  -> cannot detect conflicts

Vector: V = per-node counters
  A -> B  iff  V_A <= V_B (all components) and V_A != V_B
  A || B  iff  incomparable  -> CONCURRENT detected
  -> can detect conflicts (Dynamo/Riak)

Cost: Lamport O(1), Vector O(N)
```

### Q3. Why do vector clocks require O(N) space per event, and what compressed variants exist?
**Answer:** A vector clock has one entry per node in the system, so storing or transmitting it costs O(N) bytes (typically 4-8 bytes per entry, so 32-64 bytes for an 8-node cluster, 4-8 KB for a 1000-node cluster). At high write throughput this is significant: a key-value store with 1M writes/sec and 1000 nodes spends 4-8 GB/sec on clock metadata alone. Compressed variants address this: (1) **Version Vectors** track only entries for nodes that have written to a specific key, not the entire cluster — useful when keys have a small set of replicating nodes; (2) **Dotted Version Vectors (DVV)** pair a cluster-wide version number with a per-replica "dot" — only the dot changes per write, giving O(1) for the common case of a single writer and O(replicas) for concurrent writes; (3) **Interval Tree Clocks** allow nodes to join and leave without rebuilding all vectors, by treating each clock as a range-based interval that can be split and merged; (4) **Hashed Vector Clocks** hash node ids into a smaller bit-vector and accept some probability of false concurrency detection. Riak and Cassandra have used DVVs in production. The trade-off across all variants is between precision (exact concurrency detection) and resource cost; for small clusters (N < 50) plain vector clocks are fine, while large clusters need a compressed variant or hybrid clocks.
**Visual:**
```
Plain vector clock (N=1000): [c1,c2,...,c1000] -> 4-8 KB per event
Version Vector: only entries for replicating nodes of THIS key -> O(replicas)
DVV: {cluster_version, (replica, dot)} -> O(1) common, O(replicas) worst
Interval Tree Clock: ranges, supports join/leave -> O(log N) typical
Hashed: 64-bit Bloom-like -> O(1) but false concurrency possible

Production: Riak uses DVV; Cassandra moved to timestamps for perf
```

### Q4. In Amazon Dynamo, how are vector clocks used to detect conflicting writes, and how does the application reconcile them?
**Answer:** Dynamo attaches a vector clock to every version of every key. When a client writes a key, it provides the context (the vector clock from its last read, or empty for a new key). The coordinator node increments its own entry in the clock and stores the new value alongside the clock. When a subsequent read arrives, Dynamo collects all versions of the key from the quorum; if any two versions have incomparable clocks (neither dominates the other), they are concurrent writes — Dynamo returns both as **siblings** to the client, along with their vector clocks. The client's application code decides how to merge: for a shopping cart, set union (Alice adds milk offline, Bob adds bread offline, the merged cart has both); for a counter, sum minus shared ancestors; for a text field, last-writer-wins by some tiebreaker (lossy). After merging, the client writes the merged value back with a new vector clock derived from the join of the siblings' clocks. This is the explicit conflict-resolution contract exposed by Riak (Dynamo's open-source descendant): the application receives `siblings` and must reconcile. Dynamo's paper notes that for the shopping cart use case, the merge is naturally union and lossless; for other use cases, the application defines the merge semantics. The architect's lesson: vector clocks detect conflicts; the application resolves them; choosing the right merge function (a CRDT where possible) determines whether the system converges correctly.
**Visual:**
```
Dynamo write/read with conflict:
  T1: client reads key K -> context=VC1, value="milk"
  T2: client A writes K="milk,bread" with context=VC1 -> stored (clock VC2)
  T3: client B writes K="milk,eggs" with context=VC1 (concurrent!) -> stored (clock VC3)
       (A and B both read VC1, both wrote without seeing each other)
  T4: client reads K -> Dynamo sees VC2 || VC3 -> returns BOTH as siblings
       sibling1: "milk,bread" (VC2)
       sibling2: "milk,eggs" (VC3)
  T5: client merges -> "milk,bread,eggs", writes with context=join(VC2,VC3)
       -> new clock VC4 dominates both, conflict resolved
```

### Q5. Why is "last-writer-wins" (LWW) lossy, and when is it acceptable despite vector clocks detecting concurrency?
**Answer:** LWW resolves concurrent writes by picking the one with the highest timestamp (physical or logical) and discarding the others. This is **lossy** because the discarded writes' data is gone: if Alice and Bob concurrently add items to a shared shopping cart (Alice adds milk, Bob adds bread), LWW keeps one (say bread) and loses the other (milk) — the cart is wrong. The application's intent (union of additions) is violated. Vector clocks would detect the concurrency and let the application union them, preserving both. LWW is acceptable when (1) the data is genuinely overwriting (e.g., a user profile field where the latest edit wins by intent); (2) the cost of conflict resolution outweighs the cost of occasional loss (e.g., a low-stakes cache entry); (3) the system can tolerate eventual correction by other means (e.g., a separate reconciliation job). Cassandra chose LWW by default for performance — vector clocks' O(N) metadata was too expensive at its target write throughput, and most use cases (time-series metrics, user profile updates) tolerate LWW. Riak chose vector clocks (DVVs) by default because its target use cases (shopping carts, session state) cannot tolerate LWW. The architect's choice: LWW for performance-critical, overwrite-style data; vector clocks + application merge for collaborative, additive, or money-related data.
**Visual:**
```
Concurrent writes to K (shopping cart):
  A writes K=["milk"]    (clock VC_A)
  B writes K=["bread"]   (clock VC_B), VC_A || VC_B

Vector + app merge: K=["milk","bread"]  -> lossless
LWW:                K=["bread"]         -> milk LOST (lossy)

LWW ok: user profile "name", overwrite semantics
LWW bad: shopping cart, set-add semantics; counter; document edit
Cassandra = LWW by default (perf); Riak = DVV by default (correctness)
```

### Q6. How do vector clocks handle dynamic membership — nodes joining and leaving the cluster?
**Answer:** Plain vector clocks assume a fixed, known set of nodes: each event's vector has one entry per node, and adding or removing a node requires resizing every existing vector, which is impractical. Production systems handle dynamic membership in several ways: (1) **Version Vectors with exceptions** track only the nodes that have actually written to a key, so new nodes start contributing entries only on their first write — this works for key-value stores where each key has a small replicating set; (2) **Dotted Version Vectors (DVV)** separate a cluster-wide version from per-replica dots, so a new replica just gets a new dot without resizing historical vectors; (3) **Interval Tree Clocks** represent clocks as intervals over an ID space, allowing a node's clock to be split (join) or merged (leave) without affecting others; (4) **Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)** abandon vector structure and use physical time + a logical counter, sidestepping membership entirely at the cost of losing concurrency detection. Riak 2.0 introduced DVV specifically to handle its dynamic membership use cases (nodes being added/removed under load). The architect's rule: if your cluster membership is stable and small (N < 50), plain vector clocks are fine; if it is dynamic or large, use DVV, ITC, or HLC.
**Visual:**
```
Fixed membership (plain VC): each event has N entries; resize on add/remove = impractical

Version Vectors: track only nodes that wrote THIS key (small set)
DVV: {cluster_version, [(replica,dot),...]} -> new replica = new dot, no resize
ITC: clocks as intervals over ID space -> split on join, merge on leave
HLC: physical_time + counter -> no membership, no concurrency detection

Production: Riak uses DVV; CockroachDB uses HLC; small clusters use plain VC
```

### Q7. What is a CRDT, and how does it relate to vector clocks?
**Answer:** A CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type) is a data structure whose merge function is associative, commutative, and idempotent, guaranteeing that concurrent updates by different replicas converge to the same state deterministically. Examples: G-Set (grow-only set, merge = union), PN-Counter (positive-negative counter, merge = component-wise max of positives and negatives), LWW-Register (merge by max timestamp), OR-Set (observed-remove set, merge = union with tombstone tracking). The relationship to vector clocks is symbiotic: vector clocks **detect** concurrency, CRDTs **resolve** it. A non-CRDT merge (e.g., LWW on a text field) loses data; a CRDT merge (e.g., OR-Set union) preserves all information. Systems like Riak, Redis CRDT (Active-Active), and Yjs (collaborative editing) combine vector clocks (or DVVs) with CRDTs to provide automatic, lossless convergence. Without vector clocks, the system cannot tell which updates are concurrent (so it cannot trigger the CRDT merge correctly). Without CRDTs, vector clocks just expose conflicts that the application must hand-code merges for. Together they provide strong eventual consistency: any two replicas that have received the same set of updates (regardless of order) will have identical state. The architect's lesson: if your data type can be modeled as a CRDT, use one — vector clocks + CRDT gives automatic convergence with no application-level conflict resolution.
**Visual:**
```
Vector clocks DETECT concurrency (A || B)
CRDTs RESOLVE concurrency (lossless merge)

G-Set: {a,b} || {b,c} -> merge = {a,b,c}  (lossless, commutative)
PN-Counter: inc(x) || dec(x) -> merge = component-wise max  (lossless)
LWW-Register: x=1 || x=2 -> merge = max(ts) -> x=2  (LOSSY for the loser)
OR-Set: add(a) || remove(a) -> observed-remove -> a stays if add not seen by remove

Production: Riak + CRDTs, Redis CRDT, Yjs, Automerge
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are building a collaborative document editor (like Google Docs). Two users edit offline, then reconnect. How do you detect and merge their edits?
**Answer:** Each user's client maintains a vector clock. Every keystroke (or batch of edits) is an event that increments the client's entry in its local vector. When the user reconnects, the client sends its full edit log with vector clocks to the server, which already holds the document state with its own vector clock. The server compares each incoming edit's vector against the document's vector: edits that happen-before the document's state are already applied (discard); edits that are concurrent are merged. The merge function depends on the data model: for plain text, you would use Operational Transform (OT) or a sequence CRDT (like RGA or LSEQ) where each character is an operation with a vector clock and a position, and concurrent inserts are ordered by a deterministic tiebreaker (e.g., (vector, node_id)). For structured data (JSON), use a CRDT library (Yjs, Automerge) that handles the merge automatically. The key insight: the document is a CRDT, vector clocks detect which edits are concurrent, and the CRDT merge is by construction commutative so concurrent edits converge identically on all replicas. The architect's checklist: assign each client a unique node_id; attach a vector clock to each edit; on sync, identify concurrent edits via vector comparison; merge via CRDT; broadcast the merged state with the joined vector clock. The result is eventually consistent convergence with no data loss.
**Visual:**
```
Alice offline: edits -> [ins("H",vc1), ins("i",vc2), ...] vcAlice=[5,0]
Bob   offline: edits -> [ins("Hi",vc3), ins("!",vc4)]    vcBob  =[0,4]

Server has doc vc=[0,0]; Alice syncs -> apply Alice's edits -> doc vc=[5,0]
Bob syncs -> server compares each Bob edit's vc vs doc vc=[5,0]:
   edit vc=[0,1]: incomparable with [5,0] -> CONCURRENT -> CRDT merge
   edit vc=[0,4]: incomparable with [5,0] -> CONCURRENT -> CRDT merge
merge result (sequence CRDT): "Hi!" + Alice's "Hi" -> "HiHi!" or interleaved
                                                                 by tiebreak
final doc vc = join([5,0],[0,4]) = [5,4]
```

### Q2. A Dynamo-style key-value store returns two siblings on read for the same key. Walk through the conflict resolution.
**Answer:** The two siblings mean the store detected concurrent writes via vector clocks — neither sibling's vector dominates the other. The client receives both values with their respective vector clocks (e.g., sibling1 = "cart:milk", VC1 = {A:2,B:1}; sibling2 = "cart:bread", VC2 = {A:1,B:2}). The client application decides the merge based on the data's semantics. For a shopping cart, the merge is set union: the resolved cart is {milk, bread}. The client then writes the merged value back to the store, providing a context equal to the join (per-component max) of the two siblings' clocks: VC_merged = {A:2, B:2}. The store's coordinator increments its own entry in this clock and stores the new value with the new clock (e.g., {A:3, B:2} if the coordinator is node A). Subsequent reads return a single value (the merged cart) with the new clock. If a third concurrent write arrives with an older context, the store will create a new sibling set — the merge process repeats. The architect's lesson: the application's merge function must be associative and idempotent (a CRDT) so that repeated sibling resolutions converge; otherwise, you risk oscillating state or lost updates. For non-CRDT data (e.g., a text field), the typical fallback is LWW by physical timestamp, which is lossy.
**Visual:**
```
siblings:
  S1 = "cart:milk"  (VC1 = {A:2, B:1})
  S2 = "cart:bread" (VC2 = {A:1, B:2})  -> VC1 || VC2 (concurrent)

client merge (shopping cart semantics): cart = {milk, bread}
context to write back = join(VC1, VC2) = {A:2, B:2}

coordinator (node A) increments own -> stores with VC3 = {A:3, B:2}
  value = "cart:milk,bread"

next read -> single value, no siblings -> conflict resolved
```

### Q3. Your Cassandra cluster shows occasional lost writes. The team suspects the LWW-by-timestamp policy. How do you diagnose and fix?
**Answer:** Cassandra's default conflict resolution is last-writer-wins by the cell's timestamp, which is the coordinator's wall clock at write time. Lost writes happen when two clients write the same cell concurrently and one client's clock is behind — its write gets the older timestamp and is silently discarded. Diagnose by inspecting the raw timestamps on the cells (via `nodetool getendpoints` + a debug query, or by reading at QUORUM and checking the `writetime` returned) and comparing to the client machine clocks. If the losing write has an older timestamp, clock skew is the cause. Fixes, in order of preference: (1) **use application-provided timestamps** with `USING TIMESTAMP` so the application controls ordering independent of coordinator clock — but this still loses one of two concurrent writes; (2) **switch the data model to a CRDT-friendly form**: for counters use Cassandra's counter type (which uses a special commutative replication, not LWW); for sets use the `set` type with `add`/`remove` (which are union/difference, not LWW); for lists use the `list` type with append (which is append-only); (3) **migrate the affected keys to Riak or a CRDT-aware store** that uses vector clocks + CRDT merge for true lossless concurrency; (4) **use lightweight transactions (PAXOS-based)** for the affected writes — this serializes them at the cost of 4 round trips and lower throughput. The architect's lesson: Cassandra is tuned for LWW-friendly workloads (time series, profile fields); if your workload has additive concurrency (carts, counters, edits), either model it with CRDT-friendly types or pick a different store.
**Visual:**
```
Client A: write K=1 at T=100 (A's clock correct)
Client B: write K=2 at T=98  (B's clock 2ms slow)
Both writes reach replicas; on read, Cassandra picks cell with max(writetime)
   -> K=1 wins, K=2 silently LOST

Diagnosis: query writetime on the cell -> see T=100, compare to client clocks
Fixes:
  (1) USING TIMESTAMP <app-controlled> -> controls order, still LWW
  (2) use counter type / set type / list type (CRDT-friendly)
  (3) migrate to Riak (DVV + CRDT)
  (4) LWT (Paxos) for the few affected keys -> serial, slow
```

### Q4. You are designing a distributed counter (e.g., page-view counts). Can you use vector clocks? What are the alternatives?
**Answer:** Vector clocks alone do not help with counters because counters require merging concurrent increments by **sum**, not by max — but vector clocks only detect concurrency, they do not implement merge. The right approach is a CRDT counter: a **PN-Counter** (positive-negative counter) consists of two G-Counters (grow-only), one for increments and one for decrements; each replica maintains its own component, and the counter's value is `sum(inc) - sum(dec)`. Vector clocks (or DVVs) tag each update so the system can recognize concurrent updates and route them through the PN-Counter merge (component-wise max of each replica's counter). Cassandra's `counter` type is exactly this PN-Counter pattern under the hood. Riak's DataType counters are also PN-Counters built on DVVs. Alternatives to consider: (1) **HBase's checkAndPut** for low-throughput counters — uses a single-region strong consistency, no vector clocks needed; (2) **sharded counters** (Google's App Engine pattern) — split the counter across N shards, each updated independently, sum on read; no concurrency control needed because each shard has a single writer at a time; (3) **approximate counters** (HyperLogLog, Count-Min Sketch) for very high throughput where exact counts are not needed. The architect's choice: for exact counts at moderate throughput with multi-writer, use PN-Counter (Cassandra counter type or Riak DataType); for extreme throughput with approximation tolerance, use sharded or sketch-based counters.
**Visual:**
```
Naive (wrong): counter K with LWW -> 5 || 7 -> max=7 -> LOST the +5 (or +2)
Vector clocks detect 5 || 7 but don't tell you the merge is sum

PN-Counter (CRDT):
  inc[A]=3, inc[B]=2  -> A saw 3 increments of its own, B saw 2
  merge: max component-wise -> inc[A]=3, inc[B]=2 -> sum = 5
  dec[A]=1, dec[B]=0  -> final = 3+2 - 1 - 0 = 4 (exact, lossless)

Alternatives:
  - sharded counter: 10 shards, each single-writer -> no concurrency issue
  - HyperLogLog: approximate cardinality, very high throughput
```

### Q5. A gossip-based replicated cache shows occasional "flicker" — values oscillate between two states. How would you diagnose and fix this?
**Answer:** The flicker is almost certainly an LWW conflict with clock skew causing non-monotonic resolution. In a gossip cache, each replica writes locally and gossips updates; if two replicas write the same key concurrently and the cache resolves by LWW using wall-clock timestamps, a replica with a slow clock can lose its write to a replica with a faster clock even though both writes are valid. Worse, if the clocks oscillate (NTP corrections, VM pauses), the "winner" can flip back and forth, causing the visible flicker. Diagnose by adding logging of the timestamp and source-replica of each update, then plotting the timestamps; if you see non-monotonic timestamps on the same key, clock skew is the cause. Fixes: (1) **switch to vector clocks** with a CRDT merge — for a register (single value) use LWW-Register with a vector clock tiebreaker (max vector, then node_id), which guarantees monotonic convergence; (2) **use a hybrid logical clock (HLC)** that combines physical time with a logical counter — the logical counter ensures monotonicity even if physical time jumps; (3) **redesign the cache to use read-repair and anti-entropy with vector clocks** (read-repair on read detects siblings and merges; anti-entropy periodically syncs replicas via Merkle trees); (4) **accept LWW but bound clock skew** (run chronyd/NTP tightly, monitor drift, fail writes when drift > threshold). For a cache where exact convergence matters (e.g., feature flags, session state), use vector clocks + LWW-Register; for a cache where approximation is fine, accept LWW but warn the team about the flicker risk.
**Visual:**
```
T=100ms  Replica A writes K=v1 (A's clock correct)
T=98ms   Replica B writes K=v2 (B's clock 2ms slow)
gossip merge: max(100, 98) = 100 -> K=v1 wins

T=200ms  NTP correction on A jumps clock back to T=199
T=199ms  Replica A writes K=v3 (same key, new value)
gossip merge: max(199, 100) = 199 -> K=v3 wins
... but later B's clock catches up and B writes again with T=201 -> flips back

Fix: vector clock + LWW-Register -> tiebreak by (vector, node_id) -> monotonic
     or HLC -> physical + logical counter -> never decreases
```

### Q6. You must add vector clocks to a system with 10,000 nodes. The team says O(N) per event is too expensive. What do you propose?
**Answer:** At N=10,000, a plain vector clock is 40-80 KB per event — clearly infeasible at any meaningful throughput. The right approach is **Dotted Version Vectors (DVV)** combined with **per-key replication-set scoping**. The key insight is that in a key-value store, each key is typically replicated to only 3-5 nodes (not all 10,000), so the vector clock only needs entries for those 3-5 replicating nodes, not the entire cluster. DVV goes further: it tracks a single cluster-wide version plus per-replica "dots," so a single-writer key has O(1) metadata, and only concurrent writes bump to O(replicas) ~ 3-5 entries. For keys with truly global concurrency (rare), you can use **hashed vector clocks** — hash node ids into a fixed-size bit vector (e.g., 64 bits) and accept a small probability of false concurrency detection (treat two events as concurrent when they are actually causal). For metadata-poor systems, **Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)** abandon vector structure entirely: each event carries a (physical_time, logical_counter) pair, costing O(1) — but loses concurrency detection. The architect's recommendation: use DVV with per-key replication scoping (3-5 entries per key) for the common case; fall back to HLC for high-throughput keys where exact concurrency detection is not needed; reserve plain vector clocks for small coordination groups (e.g., the 5-node Raft consensus core). This layered approach gives vector-clock precision where it matters and HLC efficiency where it does not.
**Visual:**
```
N=10,000 nodes -> plain VC = 40-80 KB per event -> INFEASIBLE

DVV (per-key, replicas=3-5):
  {cluster_version, [(replica, dot), ...]} -> O(1) single-writer, O(5) concurrent
  -> Riak production-proven at scale

HLC (Hybrid Logical Clock):
  (physical_time_ms, counter) -> O(1) always -> no concurrency detection
  -> CockroachDB, MongoDB sharded clusters

Hashed VC:
  64-bit Bloom-like bitvector -> O(1), false concurrency possible
  -> acceptable for caches, not for ledgers

Architect: DVV for KV-store, HLC for high-throughput logs, plain VC for Raft core
```

### Q7. You are migrating a Dynamo-style store from LWW to vector-clock-based conflict detection. What changes, and how do you migrate existing data?
**Answer:** The migration has three components: schema, write path, and read path. **Schema**: add a `vector_clock` column (a serialized map of node_id -> counter) to each row; for existing rows, populate it with a synthetic vector based on the existing timestamp (e.g., {coordinator_node: timestamp}), so existing data has a baseline clock. **Write path**: on each write, the coordinator reads the existing row's vector clock, increments its own entry, and stores the new value with the updated clock; if the client provides a context (vector clock from its prior read), the coordinator verifies the context dominates the stored clock (if not, this is a stale write — proceed as concurrent write creating a sibling). **Read path**: on read, the coordinator collects versions from the quorum; if multiple versions have incomparable vector clocks, return all of them as siblings (new behavior — the client must handle a list of values, not just one). **Migration**: existing data with synthetic clocks will look "older" than any new write, so new writes will dominate cleanly; no siblings will appear for old-vs-new conflicts (old loses, which is correct). For client compatibility, introduce a feature flag: existing clients see LWW-resolved single values; new clients opt into receiving siblings. Run a backfill job to populate the `vector_clock` column for all existing rows. Roll out the write-path change first (writes start emitting clocks), then the read-path change for opted-in clients, then deprecate LWW. The architect's checklist: schema migration, write path update, read path opt-in, backfill, client SDK update, feature flag, gradual rollout, monitor sibling rates.
**Visual:**
```
Schema:  ALTER TABLE kv ADD COLUMN vector_clock BYTES;

Existing row: K=v1, ts=100 -> backfill vc={coordinator:100} (synthetic)
New write:    K=v2 with context={coordinator:100}
  coordinator reads vc={coordinator:100}, increments own -> vc={A:101}
  stores K=v2, vc={A:101} -> dominates existing -> replaces

Concurrent:  client1 reads K=v2 (vc={A:101}), writes K=v3 with vc1
             client2 reads K=v2 (vc={A:101}), writes K=v4 with vc2 (concurrent)
  store creates siblings: [(v3,vc3), (v4,vc4)] -> client gets list on read

Rollout: feature flag, opt-in clients, monitor sibling rate, deprecate LWW
```

quiz.explanation: LWW resolves concurrent writes by picking the one with the highest timestamp (physical or logical) and discarding the others. This is lossy because the discarded writes' data is gone: if Alice and Bob concurrently add items to a shared shopping cart (Alice adds milk, Bob adds bread), LWW keeps one (say bread) and loses the other (milk) — the cart is wrong. The application's intent (union of additions) is violated.
